nameStory: This tiny sea snail bears the name of someone called 'Bush' - likely a marine biologist or shell collector who first studied or collected specimens of this species. Like many scientific names, 'bushiana' honors a person who contributed to our understanding of marine life, though the exact story of this particular Bush has been lost to time.
description: Bush's Turbonille is a microscopic sea snail that lives in New England's coastal waters. This marine gastropod (the scientific term for snails and their relatives) belongs to the pyramid snail family, named for their characteristic cone-shaped shells. At less than a few millimeters long, you'd need a magnifying glass or microscope to appreciate its delicate spiral shell. Like other pyramid snails, it's a parasite that feeds on marine worms and other sea creatures.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Tiny conical shell twisted in a tall, narrow spiral like a miniature ice cream cone, smooth to the touch when handled carefully

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small - typically just a few millimeters long, about the size of a grain of rice or smaller

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Translucent white to pale cream colored shell that may appear glassy when wet

idTips.label: Habitat Location
idTips.description: Found in sandy or muddy marine sediments, often buried just beneath the surface where you might feel the shell as a tiny hard grain

habitat: Bush's Turbonille lives in the sandy and muddy bottoms of New England's shallow coastal waters and bays. You're most likely to encounter empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, mixed in with other tiny shell fragments in the wrack line. Living specimens burrow in soft marine sediments where they parasitize marine worms.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells may wash ashore on beaches as winter storms subside and spring tides move sediments around.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for beachcombing to find shells, as calmer waters allow for better searching through sand and shell debris.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity may bring more shells to shore as wave action increases and disturbs bottom sediments.
seasonality.winter: Harsh weather limits opportunities to search, though major storms may deposit shells in new locations along the shore.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny, Bush's Turbonille is a fierce parasite that drills into marine worms with a needle-like feeding tube, essentially turning its host into a living juice box that it sips from without killing immediately!
confusionNotes: With only one recorded observation in New England, this species is so rare that confusion with other organisms is unlikely. Any tiny spiral shell you find is more likely to be a young periwinkle, slipper shell, or other common marine snail.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England (only one recorded observation) means that any sighting would be scientifically significant. Most pyramid snails require microscopic examination by experts to identify to species level, so don't expect to confidently identify this in the field.
compareHints: Bush's Turbonille differs from its relative the Interrupted Turbonille by having a smoother shell surface without the distinctive bands or interruptions that give the latter species its name. Both are extremely small pyramid snails, but the Interrupted Turbonille shows clear breaks or bands in its shell pattern that Bush's Turbonille lacks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative Bush's turbonille (Turbonilla bushiana), the interrupted turbonille shows those distinctive broken or discontinuous patterns on its shell surface.
